reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO & national toxicology guidance
clinicalPearls: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with far greater affinity than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and causing profound tissue hypoxia despite a normal arterial oxygen tension
Symptoms are non-specific (headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion) and are frequently misdiagnosed as viral illness or food poisoning, especially when several household members are affected
Standard pulse oximetry is misleading because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin; a co-oximeter or blood carboxyhaemoglobin level is required
The classic cherry-red skin appearance is uncommon and unreliable, and its absence does not exclude poisoning
The cornerstone of treatment is high-flow 100 percent oxygen, which greatly shortens the elimination half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is considered for severe poisoning (loss of consciousness, neurological signs, cardiac involvement, pregnancy, or very high levels) to reduce delayed neurological sequelae
Delayed neuropsychiatric syndrome (cognitive impairment, movement disorders, personality change) can develop days to weeks after apparent recovery
Suspect concurrent cyanide poisoning in victims of smoke inhalation from enclosed-space fires
reference.pathophysiology: Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas produced by incomplete combustion. It binds haemoglobin with roughly 200-250 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, which both reduces oxygen-carrying capacity and shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve leftward, impairing oxygen release to tissues. CO also binds myoglobin and inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia and oxidative stress. The brain and heart, with high oxygen demand, are most vulnerable, and a lipid peroxidation and inflammatory cascade underlies the delayed neurological injury.
additionalInvestigations: Blood carboxyhaemoglobin level by co-oximetry (venous or arterial)
Arterial blood gas with metabolic acidosis and lactate
ECG and cardiac biomarkers to detect myocardial ischaemia
Neuroimaging in severe cases (basal ganglia changes)
Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age given fetal risk
redFlags: Any loss of consciousness, seizure, or focal neurological deficit
Chest pain, arrhythmia, or ECG evidence of ischaemia
Metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate indicating severe tissue hypoxia
Pregnancy, as the fetus is disproportionately affected
Multiple people from the same environment falling ill simultaneously
reference.prognosis: Mild poisoning usually resolves fully with oxygen, but severe exposure can cause death or lasting neurological and cardiac damage; delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae may appear after seemingly complete recovery, and early high-flow or hyperbaric oxygen reduces this risk.
pitfalls: Trusting a normal pulse oximeter reading and normal arterial oxygen tension to exclude poisoning
Attributing symptoms to a viral illness and discharging the patient back to the source
Relying on the cherry-red sign, which is usually absent
Overlooking coexisting cyanide toxicity in fire victims
management: Immediate removal from the source and high-flow 100 percent oxygen by non-rebreather mask to accelerate carboxyhaemoglobin elimination
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy considered for severe poisoning, including loss of consciousness, neurological or cardiac involvement, or pregnancy
Continuous cardiac monitoring with ECG and cardiac biomarkers to detect myocardial ischaemia
Measurement and serial monitoring of carboxyhaemoglobin by co-oximetry to guide the duration of oxygen therapy
Supportive care with correction of metabolic acidosis and management of seizures
Prioritisation of the pregnant patient, continuing oxygen longer given foetal susceptibility
Follow-up for delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae and advice on source identification and prevention, including CO alarms and appliance servicing
